The intersection of a random plane conic \(Q\) with the smooth cubic \(C\) has degree  

\[
\deg C\cdot \deg Q = 3\cdot 2 = 6 .
\]

For a conic that meets \(C\) transversely the six intersection points are distinct.  
Let  

\[
\mathcal Q_p=\{ \text{non‑zero quadratic forms in }x,y,z\}/\mathbb F_p^\times ,
\qquad |\mathcal Q_p| = \frac{p^{6}-1}{p-1}=p^{5}+p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

For a fixed \(\mathbb F_p\)-rational point \(P\in C(\mathbb F_p)\) the condition “\(P\in Q\)” is a single linear equation on the six coefficients of the quadratic form, so the subspace of forms vanishing at \(P\) has dimension \(5\). Hence the number of conics containing \(P\) is  

\[
\frac{p^{5}-1}{p-1}=p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

Thus  

\[
\Pr(P\in Q)=\frac{p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1}{p^{5}+p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1}
          = \frac{1}{p}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right).
\]

Let \(N_p(Q)\) be the number of \(\mathbb F_p\)-points of \(C\cap Q\).  
By linearity of expectation,

\[
\mathbb E[N_p]=\sum_{P\in C(\mathbb F_p)}\Pr(P\in Q)
            = |C(\mathbb F_p)|\;\Pr(P\in Q).
\]

For a smooth cubic (genus 1) the Hasse–Weil bound gives  

\[
|C(\mathbb F_p)| = p+1-a_p,\qquad |a_p|\le 2\sqrt p .
\]

Hence  

\[
\mathbb E[N_p]=\frac{p+1-a_p}{p}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)
              = 1 + O\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt p}\right).
\]

The restriction to transverse conics removes only those conics that are tangent at a point of \(C\); the tangency condition imposes an extra linear equation, so the proportion of such conics is \(O(1/p)\) and does not affect the limit.

Therefore  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty} A(p)=\lim_{p\to\infty}\mathbb E[N_p]=1 .
\]

Rounded to four decimal places, the limiting value is  

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

The average number of \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-points in the transverse intersection of the cubic  
\(C:\;x^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}=0\) with a random plane conic can be computed by linearity of expectation.

For each \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-point \(P\in C(\mathbb{F}_p)\) the probability that a random conic (up to scalar) passes through \(P\) is the proportion of quadratic forms vanishing at \(P\).  
Quadratic forms in three variables form a 6‑dimensional vector space; the condition “\(Q(P)=0\)” is a single linear equation, so the subspace has dimension 5. Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(P\in Q\bigr)=\frac{p^{5}-1}{p^{6}-1}\cdot\frac{p-1}{p-1}
      =\frac{p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1}{p^{5}+p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1}
      =\frac{1}{p}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right).
\]

Summing over all \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-points of the cubic gives

\[
A(p)=\sum_{P\in C(\mathbb{F}_p)}\Pr(P\in Q)
    =|C(\mathbb{F}_p)|\left(\frac{1}{p}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)\right).
\]

For a smooth cubic, Hasse–Weil yields \(|C(\mathbb{F}_p)| = p+1+O(\sqrt{p})\). Therefore

\[
A(p)=\bigl(p+1+O(\sqrt{p})\bigr)\left(\frac{1}{p}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)\right)
     =1+O\!\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{p}}\right).
\]

Consequently,

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty} A(p)=1.
\]

Rounded to four decimal places, the limiting value is

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

The intersection divisor of a conic \(Q\) with the cubic \(C\) has degree  

\[
\deg(C\cap Q)=3\cdot 2 = 6 .
\]

For a smooth cubic \(C\) (an elliptic curve) the restriction of the line bundle \(\mathcal O_{\mathbf P^{2}}(2)\) to \(C\) is a line bundle of degree \(6\).  
Its complete linear system \(|2H|\) has dimension  

\[
h^{0}(C,\mathcal O_{C}(2H))-1 = 6-1 =5 ,
\]

so the space of conics (up to scaling) \(\mathbf P^{5}(\mathbb F_{p})\) parametrises exactly the complete linear system \(|2H|\).  
Thus a random conic corresponds to a random effective divisor \(D\) of degree \(6\) in \(|2H|\).

For a divisor \(D\) of degree \(6\) the Frobenius automorphism of \(\mathbb F_{p}\) permutes the six geometric points of \(D\).  
The monodromy group of the linear system \(|2H|\) on an elliptic curve is the full symmetric group \(S_{6}\); consequently, as \(p\to\infty\) the Frobenius permutation becomes equidistributed in \(S_{6}\).

For a uniformly random permutation \(\sigma\in S_{6}\) the expected number of fixed points is

\[
\mathbb{E}[\text{fixed points}] = \sum_{i=1}^{6}\Pr(\sigma(i)=i)=6\cdot\frac{1}{6}=1 .
\]

A fixed point of the Frobenius permutation is precisely an \(\mathbb F_{p}\)-rational point of the intersection \(C\cap Q\).  
Hence the expected number of \(\mathbb F_{p}\)-rational points in the transverse intersection of a random conic with \(C\) tends to \(1\) as \(p\) grows.

Therefore  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty} A(p)=1.
\]

Rounded to four decimal places:

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

\mathcal{Q}_p=\{ \text{quadratic forms }Q(x,y,z)\in\mathbf{F}_p[x,y,z]\;|\; Q\neq 0\}/\mathbf{F}_p^{\times}

be the set of conics (including singular ones).

\[

               = \frac{p^{6}-1}{p-1}=p^{5}+p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

### Probability that a random conic passes through a given point  

Fix a point \(P\in\mathbf{P}^2(\mathbf{F}_p)\).  
The condition \(Q(P)=0\) is a single linear equation on the coefficients of \(Q\); hence the conics containing \(P\) form a projective subspace \(\mathbf{P}^4(\mathbf{F}_p)\) of size  

\[
\frac{p^{5}-1}{p-1}=p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

Therefore  

\[
\Pr_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}_p}\bigl(P\in Q\bigr)=
\frac{p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1}{p^{5}+p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1}
= \frac{1}{p}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right).
\]

---

### Expected number of \(\mathbf{F}_p\)-points in \(C\cap Q\)

Let \(C\) be the smooth cubic \(x^{3}+y^{3}+z^{3}=0\).  
By the Hasse bound  

\[
|C(\mathbf{F}_p)| = p+1-t,\qquad |t|\le 2\sqrt{p},
\]

so \(|C(\mathbf{F}_p)| = p+1+O(\sqrt{p})\).

For a conic \(Q\) that meets \(C\) transversely (the non‑transverse cases are \(O(1/p)\) of all conics, hence negligible for the limit), the number of \(\mathbf{F}_p\)-points in the intersection is  

\[
N_p(Q)=\#\{P\in C(\mathbf{F}_p): P\in Q\}.
\]

Using linearity of expectation,

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}\bigl[N_p(Q)\bigr]
&= \sum_{P\in C(\mathbf{F}_p)} \Pr(P\in Q)  \\
&= |C(\mathbf{F}_p)|\left(\frac{1}{p}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)\right) \\
&= (p+1+O(\sqrt{p}))\left(\frac{1}{p}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)\right) \\
&= 1 + O\!\left(\frac{1}{p}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]

Thus  

\[
A(p)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}_p|}\sum_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}_p} N_p(Q)
      = 1 + O\!\left(\frac{1}{p}\right).
\]

\[

The space of homogeneous quadratic forms in three variables has dimension \(6\); up to non‑zero scalar multiplication the set \(\mathcal{Q}_{p}\) is the projective space \(\mathbf{P}^{5}(\mathbf{F}_{p})\) with  

\[
|\mathcal{Q}_{p}|=\frac{p^{6}-1}{p-1}=p^{5}+p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

Restricting to conics that meet the smooth cubic \(C\) transversely, each such conic gives a divisor  

\[
D=C\cap Q \in |2H|
\]

on the elliptic curve \(C\) (here \(H\) is the hyperplane divisor, \(\deg H=3\)).  
The complete linear system \(|2H|\) has degree \(6\) and dimension  

\[
h^{0}(C,\mathcal{O}_{C}(2H))-1 = 6-1 =5,
\]

so the set of divisors coming from conics is exactly the projective space \(\mathbf{P}^{5}(\mathbf{F}_{p})\).

Let \(n = \#C(\mathbf{F}_{p}) = p+1-a_{p}\) with \(|a_{p}|\le 2\sqrt{p}\).  
For a fixed rational point \(P\in C(\mathbf{F}_{p})\), the condition “\(P\) lies in the divisor” is a single linear condition on the \(6\)-dimensional space of sections of \(\mathcal{O}_{C}(2H)\). Hence the subspace of sections vanishing at \(P\) has dimension \(5\). Consequently

\[
\Pr(P\in D)=\frac{p^{5}-1}{p^{6}-1}= \frac{1}{p}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right).
\]

By linearity of expectation, the average number of \(\mathbf{F}_{p}\)-rational points on a random divisor \(D\) (hence on a random transverse conic) is  

\[
\mathbb{E}[N_{p}(Q)]=\sum_{P\in C(\mathbf{F}_{p})}\Pr(P\in D)
               = n\left(\frac{1}{p}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)\right)
               = \frac{p+1-a_{p}}{p}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{p}\right)
               = 1+O\!\left(\frac{1}{p}\right).
\]

Thus  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty} A(p)=\lim_{p\to\infty}\mathbb{E}[N_{p}(Q)]=1.
\]

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

The conics are given by quadratic forms in three variables, up to a non‑zero scalar.  
Hence the set \(\mathcal Q_p\) is the projective space \(\mathbf P^5(\mathbf F_p)\) whose size is  

\[
|\mathcal Q_p| = \frac{p^{6}-1}{p-1}=p^{5}+p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

For a fixed \(\mathbf F_p\)-point \(P\in C(\mathbf F_p)\) the condition that a conic pass through \(P\) is a single linear condition on the coefficients of the quadratic form, so the conics containing \(P\) form a \(\mathbf P^{4}(\mathbf F_p)\) of size  

\[
p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

Thus the probability that a randomly chosen conic contains a given rational point of \(C\) is  

\[
r_p=\frac{p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1}{p^{5}+p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1}
      =\frac{1}{p}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right).
\]

Let \(N_p=|C(\mathbf F_p)|\).  Since \(C\) is a smooth cubic (an elliptic curve),

\[
N_p = p+1-a_p ,\qquad |a_p|\le 2\sqrt p .
\]

Using linearity of expectation, the average number of rational intersection points is  

\[
A(p)=\frac1{|\mathcal Q_p|}\sum_{Q\in\mathcal Q_p} N_p(Q)
     = N_p\; r_p
     = (p+1-a_p)\Bigl(\frac{1}{p}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right)\Bigr)
     = 1+\frac{1-a_p}{p}+O\!\left(\frac{1}{p^{2}}\right).
\]

The term \(\frac{1-a_p}{p}\) tends to \(0\) as \(p\to\infty\) because \(|a_p|\le 2\sqrt p\).  
Conics that fail to intersect \(C\) transversely form a set of density \(O(1/p)\); conditioning on transverse intersection does not affect the limit.

Hence  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty} A(p)=1 .
\]

Rounded to four decimal places the limiting value is  

\[
\boxed{1.0000}
\]

The average can be computed by double‑counting incidences between \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)-points of the cubic and conics.

---

### 1.  Number of conics  

A homogeneous quadratic form in three variables has 6 coefficients, so the vector space of quadratic forms over \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\) has dimension \(6\).  
Modulo non‑zero scalar multiplication, the set of conics is the projective space
\[
\mathcal{Q}_{p}\cong \mathbf{P}^{5}(\mathbb{F}_{p}),
\qquad 
|\mathcal{Q}_{p}|=\frac{p^{6}-1}{p-1}=p^{5}+p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

---

### 2.  Conics through a fixed point  

Fix a rational point \(P\in C(\mathbb{F}_{p})\). Requiring a quadratic form to vanish at \(P\) imposes one independent linear condition on the six coefficients, leaving a 5‑dimensional subspace. Hence the conics containing \(P\) form \(\mathbf{P}^{4}(\mathbb{F}_{p})\) and their number is  

\[
\frac{p^{5}-1}{p-1}=p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1 .
\]

---

### 3.  Incidence count  

Let  

\[
S=\{(Q,P)\mid Q\in\mathcal{Q}_{p},\; P\in C(\mathbb{F}_{p}),\; P\in Q\}.
\]

Counting \(S\) by first fixing \(Q\) gives  

\[
|S|=\sum_{Q\in\mathcal{Q}_{p}} N_{p}(Q),
\]

where \(N_{p}(Q)\) is the number of \(\mathbb{F}_{p}\)-points of \(C\cap Q\).  

Counting \(S\) instead by first fixing a point \(P\) gives  

\[
|S|=|C(\mathbb{F}_{p})|\;\bigl(p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1\bigr).
\]

Hence  

\[
A(p)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}_{p}|}\sum_{Q}N_{p}(Q)
     =\frac{|C(\mathbb{F}_{p})|\;(p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1)}
            {p^{5}+p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1}.
\]

---

### 4.  Asymptotics of \(|C(\mathbb{F}_{p})|\)

The curve \(C\) is an elliptic curve; by the Hasse bound  

\[
|C(\mathbb{F}_{p})| = p+1-a_{p},\qquad |a_{p}|\le 2\sqrt{p}.
\]

Thus \(|C(\mathbb{F}_{p})| = p + O(\sqrt{p})\).

---

### 5.  Limit of \(A(p)\)

Insert the asymptotic expression:

\[
A(p)=\frac{(p+O(\sqrt{p}))\,(p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1)}
            {p^{5}+p^{4}+p^{3}+p^{2}+p+1}.
\]

Factor \(p^{5}\) from numerator and denominator:

\[
A(p)=\frac{p\bigl(1+O(p^{-1/2})\bigr)\,
          \bigl(1+ p^{-1}+p^{-2}+p^{-3}+p^{-4}\bigr)}
         {1+ p^{-1}+p^{-2}+p^{-3}+p^{-4}+p^{-5}}.
\]

As \(p\to\infty\) the terms \(p^{-1},p^{-2},\dots\) vanish, giving  

\[
\lim_{p\to\infty}A(p)=1.
\]

(The exclusion of singular or tangent conics changes both the numerator and denominator only by a lower‑order \(O(p^{4})\) amount, leaving the limit unchanged.)

per_skill_role.parametrize_conics_by_symmetric_matrices: Rewrite the equation $x^2+y^2=t z^2$ as the zero locus of the symmetric matrix $M(t)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&-t\end{pmatrix}$, thereby viewing $X$ as a family of plane conics parametrised by $t\in\mathbb{P}^1$.

per_skill_role.use_lang_weil_estimate_for_point_counts: Use the Lang–Weil estimate for smooth plane conics (dimension 1, degree 2) to conclude that each smooth fibre contains exactly $q+1$ $\mathbb{F}_{q}$‑points, and then combine this with the explicit count of points on the singular fibre $t=0$ to obtain the total number of points on $X$.

skill_chain_rationale: First we parametrize the conics via symmetric matrices (skill 1) to describe the family; then we invoke generic smoothness (skill 2) to identify the smooth fibres for $t\neq0$; finally we apply Lang–Weil (skill 3) to count points on those smooth fibres and combine with the singular fibre count to get the total.

When \(t=0\) the equation is \(xz=0\), i.e. the union of the two lines  

\[
L_1:\;x=0,\qquad L_2:\;z=0 .
\]

Each line in \(\mathbb{P}^{2}(\mathbb{F}_{101})\) contains \(101+1=102\) points.  
The two lines intersect in the single point \((0\!:\!1\!:\!0)\), so  

\[
N(0)=|C_0(\mathbb{F}_{101})|=2\cdot102-1=203 .
\]

---

### 2.  The case \(t\neq 0\)

For \(t\neq 0\) the conic is smooth because the gradient  

\[
(\partial_x,\partial_y,\partial_z)=(z,-2ty,x)
\]

cannot vanish simultaneously (it would force \(x=z=0\) and then \(y=0\), which is not a projective point).

A smooth plane conic over a finite field \(\mathbb{F}_q\) always has an \(\mathbb{F}_q\)-rational point (Chevalley–Warning for a quadratic form in three variables). Hence it is \(\mathbb{F}_q\)-isomorphic to \(\mathbb{P}^{1}\), and therefore

\[
|C_t(\mathbb{F}_{101})| = 101+1 = 102 \qquad\text{for every }t\neq 0 .
\]

Thus  

\[
N(t)=102\quad\text{for }t=1,2,\dots ,100 .
\]

---

### 3.  Average number of points

\[
\begin{aligned}
\text{Sum of points} &= N(0)+\sum_{t\neq 0} N(t) \\
&= 203 + 100\cdot 102 = 203 + 10200 = 10403 .
\end{aligned}
\]

The average over the \(101\) values of \(t\) is  

\[
\frac{10403}{101}=103 .
\]

---

### 4.  Rounded answer

Rounded to four decimal places the average is \(103.0000\).

\[
\boxed{103.0000}
\]
